result:
**Read it if you're building a SKILL.md linter or rubric; skim the smell list otherwise.**

The paper studies 238 popular SKILL.md files from a marketplace dump and delivers three artifacts: a component taxonomy (13 higher / 44 lower semantic components), 26 "skill smells" derived by inverting community best practices, and an LLM-judge-based detector.

**What's actually usable**

- The 26-smell catalog is a ready-made rubric. It splits cleanly into 5 static checks (word/char caps on body/name/description, backslash paths, XML in frontmatter) and 21 judge checks.
- The judge design is copyable: per-smell definition plus one positive and one negative example, binary yes/no, thinking mode on a quantized Qwen3.6-27B. Weighted F1 0.78 against 53 hand-labeled files.
- Component prevalence data shows what real skills contain: Task 74%, Introduction 64%, References 57%, then a long tail under 25%.

**Headline findings**

Over 99% of skills carry at least one smell, averaging 10.5 each; exactly one file of 238 is clean. Rationalization Loophole (nothing discourages the agent from skipping required steps) hits 94%. Smells rarely get removed once introduced. Only 7 of 13 component types have any community guidance at all.

**Why the findings are weak**

The "best practices" are folklore: top-50 web search results filtered to 29 sources, conflicts settled by majority vote, no causal validation. The paper shows smells are common, not that they hurt agent performance. A 99% prevalence rate with a 10.5 average also suggests the thresholds are tuned to flag nearly everything, which limits their value as a priority signal. Detector numbers rest on 53 labeled files and one quantized open model.

**Verdict:** read the smell catalog and the judge prompt design in full; treat every prevalence number as descriptive of a marketplace sample, not as evidence about what makes skills work.
